etymology: From the Aramaic Beth-hesda, “house of mercy” or “house of outpouring,” a pool by the sheep market in Jerusalem.
biblical_def: By the sheep market in Jerusalem stood a pool called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches, in which lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water (Joh 5:2; Joh 5:3). Among them was a certain man which had an infirmity thirty and eight years; and when Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, He saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? (Joh 5:6). The man, knowing no help but the troubled water and having no man to put him in, looked only to means that had failed him eight and thirty years; but Christ needed neither pool nor porch. He said, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk; and immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked (Joh 5:8; Joh 5:9). The dictionary marks Bethesda as a house of mercy made good by the coming of the Lord of mercy. The healing was wrought on the sabbath, that Christ might shew Himself Lord also of the sabbath; and afterward He found the man and said, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee (Joh 5:14). So the Scripture teaches that He who heals the body would heal the soul, and that long bondage to sin is no barrier to His sovereign and unbidden grace, which seeks out the helpless before ever they seek Him.
webster_summary: A pool in Jerusalem where Christ healed a man infirm thirty-eight years, bidding him rise and walk.

corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; the healing at Bethesda shews His sovereign grace seeking the helpless who could not help themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: The healing at Bethesda has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the great signs recorded in the Gospel of John. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the compassion and the divine power of Christ, who made whole a man bound thirty-eight years by a word alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freeness and sovereignty of Christ’s grace. The man at Bethesda had no man to help him and no power in himself; he looked to a troubled pool that had failed him eight and thirty years. Christ came unbidden, asked the question of mercy, and healed him by His word without pool or porch. So the dictionary draws the sign-value: as the body was made whole at His sovereign word, so the dead and helpless soul is quickened by the same word of grace, which seeks the sinner before ever the sinner seeks the Lord, and bids him sin no more.

etymology: From the Greek typhlos ek genetes, “blind from birth,” the man whose eyes Christ opened in the ninth chapter of John.
biblical_def: As Jesus passed by, He saw a man which was blind from his birth; and when His disciples asked who had sinned, this man or his parents, Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him (Joh 9:3). Then He made clay of the spittle, anointed the man’s eyes, and said, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam; and he went and washed, and came seeing (Joh 9:7). When the Pharisees, hating the sign, pressed him to disown his healer, he gave the answer that has rung down the ages: One thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see (Joh 9:25). They cast him out; but Jesus sought him, revealed Himself as the Son of God, and the man worshipped Him (Joh 9:38). The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of spiritual sight given to the blind. Christ said, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind (Joh 9:39): the beggar born blind received sight of body and soul, while the seeing Pharisees, proud in their own light, were left in their sin. So the Scripture teaches that the natural man is born blind, and only the sovereign work of Christ opens the eyes; and that the simplest testimony of a healed and seeing soul confounds the learned wisdom of the world.
webster_summary: A man blind from birth whose eyes Christ opened, made to see in body and soul as a sign of spiritual sight.

The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the divine power of Christ to give what was never possessed from birth, and the sign-value of spiritual sight bestowed on the blind.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the natural man is born spiritually blind and cannot see the kingdom of God until Christ open his eyes. So the dictionary draws the sign: as the man was given eyes he never had, so regeneration is not the mending of a faculty but the sovereign giving of sight to the blind, and the healed soul’s plain confession, now I see, confounds the wisdom of the world.

etymology: From the place-name Nain, a city of Galilee, where Christ raised the only son of a widow from the dead.
biblical_def: As Christ drew near the gate of the city called Nain, behold, there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow; and much people of the city was with her (Luk 7:12). Beholding the desolation of a woman bereft of husband and now of her only son, when the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not (Luk 7:13). Then He came and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still; and He said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak; and He delivered him to his mother (Luk 7:14; Luk 7:15). The dictionary marks the raising at Nain as the first of Christ’s raisings of the dead, and the purest display of His unbidden compassion: no man asked Him, no faith was named, but His own mercy moved Him toward a weeping widow. There came a fear on all, and they glorified God, saying, That God hath visited His people (Luk 7:16). So the Scripture teaches the divine power of Christ over death itself, who needed but a word to call the dead to life; and it sets forth the tenderness of the Lord, who turns the funeral into a resurrection, a pledge of that day when He shall call all His own from the grave by the same almighty voice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the divine compassion and resurrection power of Christ. The mourner is taught to look not to a great prophet only, but to God who hath visited His people in the person of His Son.

etymology: From Jairus (Hebrew Yair, “he will enlighten”), a ruler of the synagogue whose only daughter Christ raised from death.
biblical_def: Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, fell at Jesus’ feet and besought Him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: I pray thee, come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live (Mar 5:23). As Christ went, the woman with the issue of blood was healed by the way; and while He yet spake, there came word that the maid was dead, and that the Master should be troubled no further. But Jesus said unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe (Mar 5:36). Coming to the house and putting forth the mourners that laughed Him to scorn, He took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. And straightway the damsel arose, and walked (Mar 5:41; Mar 5:42). The dictionary marks this raising as a sign of Christ’s lordship over death, who deals with the grave as with a sleep, for He said, The damsel is not dead, but sleepeth (Mar 5:39). He took her by the hand and spake in the homely tongue of the household, calling her back as a mother wakes a sleeping child. So the Scripture teaches that faith must press through the news of death and believe still; for to the eye of Christ, death is but a sleep from which His word shall surely awaken His own at the last day.

So the dictionary draws the sign: as He took the damsel by the hand and said, Talitha cumi, so He shall at the last day take His sleeping saints by the hand and awaken them; and the believer is taught to press through the report of death and trust the Lord of life.

word: The Woman with the Issue of Blood
etymology: From the Greek for one having a rhysis haimatos, “a flowing of blood,” the woman healed by touching the hem of Christ’s garment.
biblical_def: A certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, and had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse, came in the press behind, and touched Christ’s garment (Mar 5:25; Mar 5:27). For she said, If I may touch but His clothes, I shall be whole. And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague (Mar 5:28; Mar 5:29). Jesus, knowing that virtue had gone out of Him, turned and asked who touched His clothes; and the woman, fearing and trembling, fell down before Him and told Him all the truth. And He said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague (Mar 5:34). The dictionary marks this healing as a sign of faith that lays hold on Christ even in the throng. Her cure was no magic in the cloth, for many pressed about Him and were not healed; it was faith reaching out to the power of Christ that drew the virtue forth. So the Scripture teaches that the weakest, most secret, most trembling faith, if it but touch Christ, is saving faith; and that the Lord will not leave such faith unowned, but calls the hidden believer forth to confess Him, and sends her away healed and at peace, naming her Daughter.
webster_summary: A woman healed of a twelve-year issue of blood by touching Christ’s garment in faith.

So the dictionary draws the sign: the most secret and fearful faith, if it but lay hold on the Saviour, is owned of Him; and the Lord calls the hidden believer forth, names her Daughter, and sends her away whole and in peace, that none might think her cured by chance and not by Him.

etymology: From the Latin centurio, a Roman officer over a hundred men, whose servant Christ healed at a word for the master’s great faith.
biblical_def: There came unto Christ a centurion, beseeching Him, and saying, Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented. And Jesus saith unto him, I will come and heal him (Mat 8:6; Mat 8:7). But the centurion answered, Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed (Mat 8:8). For he was a man set under authority; and he reasoned that as his own word commanded men, so the word of Christ commanded sickness and health, needing no journey but a word alone. When Jesus heard it, He marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel (Mat 8:10). And He said unto the centurion, Go thy way; and as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee. And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour (Mat 8:13). The dictionary marks this healing as the great example of faith that rests on the bare word of Christ. The man was a Gentile and a soldier, yet his faith outran that of Israel, and Christ used it to foretell that many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham in the kingdom of heaven (Mat 8:11). So the Scripture teaches the sufficiency of Christ’s word, and that true faith honours Him by trusting His word though He be not seen.

etymology: From the Greek basilikos, “a king’s officer,” whose son lay sick at Capernaum and was healed by Christ’s word at Cana.
biblical_def: There was a certain nobleman, an officer of the king, whose son was sick at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus was come out of Judaea into Galilee, he went unto Him, and besought Him that He would come down, and heal his son: for he was at the point of death (Joh 4:46; Joh 4:47). Jesus said unto him, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe (Joh 4:48), pressing the man to a faith that should rest not on the sight of a miracle but on the bare word. When the nobleman urged, Sir, come down ere my child die, Jesus saith unto him, Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way (Joh 4:50). As he was going down, his servants met him, and told him that his son lived; and inquiring the hour, he knew it was the selfsame hour in which Jesus said unto him, Thy son liveth: and himself believed, and his whole house (Joh 4:53). The dictionary marks this as the second sign Christ wrought in Galilee, a healing at a distance by His word. So the Scripture teaches that Christ would lead His people from a faith that leans on signs to a faith that rests on His word alone; and that He who spake life into a dying child fifteen miles off is the Lord whose word is life wherever it goes forth.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faith that rests on the word of Christ and not on the sight of wonders. Christ pressed the nobleman beyond a faith that must see, saying, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe; and then He gave him only the word, Thy son liveth, and the man believed it and went his way. So the dictionary draws the sign: that the bare word of Christ is life, healing a dying child fifteen miles away in the selfsame hour; and that genuine faith, tried and led on, comes at last to rest wholly on what Christ has said, so that himself believed, and his whole house.

etymology: From the Aramaic Ephphatha, “Be opened,” the word Christ spake to one deaf and having an impediment in his speech.
biblical_def: In the coasts of Decapolis they brought unto Christ one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech; and they beseech Him to put His hand upon him (Mar 7:32). Christ took him aside from the multitude, and put His fingers into his ears, and He spit, and touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, He sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened (Mar 7:33; Mar 7:34). And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain (Mar 7:35). The dictionary marks the tender manner of this healing: Christ drew the man apart, dealt with him by signs his shut senses could perceive, and sighed as one bearing in Himself the groaning of a fallen creation, before He spake the word of power. The people were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: He maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak (Mar 7:37), a saying that echoes the prophecy of the day when the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped and the tongue of the dumb sing (Isa 35:5). So the Scripture teaches the divine power and the gentle compassion of Christ together, who opens not only stopped ears but the deaf and dumb soul, that it may hear the word of God and speak His praise; for by nature men are deaf to the gospel until He say, Be opened, and the loosed tongue confess Him Lord.
webster_summary: A man deaf and dumb whom Christ healed with the word Ephphatha, Be opened, making him hear and speak plain.

corruption_paragraphs: The healing of the deaf and dumb man has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the tender signs recorded by Mark. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the gentle manner of Christ, who dealt with the man by signs his shut senses could perceive, and the power of the word that opened his ears.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ opens what is shut, both the stopped ear and the deaf and dumb soul. He sighed as one bearing the groaning of a fallen creation, then spake the word, Ephphatha, Be opened, and the man heard and spake plain, fulfilling the prophecy that the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. So the dictionary draws the sign: by nature men are deaf to the gospel and dumb in praise, until Christ say, Be opened; and when He speaks, the ears are unstopped to hear the word of God and the loosed tongue confesses Him Lord. He hath done all things well.

etymology: From Bethsaida (Aramaic, “house of fishing”), the town where Christ healed a blind man by two stages.
biblical_def: At Bethsaida they brought a blind man unto Christ, and besought Him to touch him. He took the blind man by the hand, and led him out of the town; and when He had spit on his eyes, and put His hands upon him, He asked him if he saw ought (Mar 8:22; Mar 8:23). And the man looked up, and said, I see men as trees, walking (Mar 8:24). After that He put His hands again upon his eyes, and made him look up: and he was restored, and saw every man clearly (Mar 8:25). The dictionary marks this as the only healing Christ wrought in two stages, and it was no failure of His power, but a deliberate sign. The man saw dimly first, men as trees walking, and then clearly; and the lesson stood as a parable to the disciples whose own eyes were but half opened, who saw Christ in part and yet not fully. So the Scripture teaches that the giving of spiritual sight is the work of Christ, who can do it at once or by degrees as it pleases Him; and that they whose eyes He has touched, though they yet see in part, shall not be left dim, for He who began the good work will lay His hands on again, and make them see every man clearly, until that day when we shall see, no longer through a glass darkly, but face to face.

corruption_paragraphs: The two-stage healing of the blind man of Bethsaida has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the singular sign recorded by Mark. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the deliberate manner of Christ, who healed by degrees not from weakness but to teach a lesson of dim and then clear sight.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the giving of spiritual sight is wholly Christ’s work, done at once or by degrees as it pleases Him. The man saw men as trees walking before he saw clearly, a parable to the disciples whose eyes were but half opened, who knew Christ in part and not yet fully. So the dictionary draws the sign: the believer whose eyes Christ has touched may yet see dimly, knowing in part; but He who began the work will lay His hands on again and restore him to clear sight, until that day when we shall see no longer through a glass darkly, but face to face.

etymology: From the Greek lepros, “leprous,” the ten men cleansed by Christ of whom only one returned to give thanks.
biblical_def: As Christ entered into a certain village, there met Him ten men that were lepers, which stood afar off, as the law required of the unclean; and they lifted up their voices, and said, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us (Luk 17:13). And when He saw them, He said unto them, Go shew yourselves unto the priests. And it came to pass, that, as they went, they were cleansed (Luk 17:14). They were healed in the way of obedience, believing the word. But one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and glorified God, and fell down on his face at Christ’s feet, giving Him thanks: and he was a Samaritan (Luk 17:16). And Jesus answering said, Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine? (Luk 17:17). To the one who returned He said, Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole (Luk 17:19). The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of cleansing received and thanksgiving rendered. All ten were cleansed of the body; but only one, a Samaritan and stranger, returned to glorify God, and to him alone was spoken the word of saving wholeness. So the Scripture teaches that many receive the common mercies of God and go their way unthankful, but the marks of true and saving faith are the returning heart and the glorifying tongue; for he that is healed in soul as well as body falls down at the feet of Christ, and gives Him thanks.

corruption_paragraphs: The cleansing of the ten lepers has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the tender sign recorded by Luke of mercy received and thanks rendered. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the compassion of Christ on the unclean and the rarity of the thankful heart.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that many receive the common mercies of God and depart unthankful, but saving faith returns to glorify Him. All ten were cleansed of the leprosy, healed in the way of obedience as they went; yet only one, a Samaritan and stranger, turned back, fell at Christ’s feet, and gave Him thanks, and to him alone was spoken, Thy faith hath made thee whole. So the dictionary draws the sign: bodily cleansing is given to many, but the returning heart and the glorifying tongue mark the soul that is whole indeed; and Christ’s question, Where are the nine, rebukes every receiver of mercy who forgets the Giver.
